Each deadline is evaluated separately, without a shared total token budget across deadlines. Longer calls are more likely to succeed but can increase completion time, while very short calls repeatedly incur the fixed overhead. Both allocation policies attain their shortest modeled completion time at h=2h=2 on this grid.

At h=2h=2, optimized allocation equalizes all six coverage values at approximately 0.22110.2211, whereas uniform allocation gives 0.15850.1585, 0.13590.1359, and 0.08500.0850 to the three pairs of blocks. The corresponding worst-block horizons are 19 and 52 rounds, or 45.6 and 124.8 modeled time units.

Checking the rate and merge identities.

We compare the exact mean-loss formula with 20,000 seeded independent runs at h=2h=2 over 20 rounds. The simulated normalized mean loss is 0.0063670.006367, with standard error 0.0002320.000232, compared with the exact value 0.0067520.006752. We also verify the matching decomposition used to realize the allocation.

For a six-block path with objective ∑b(1−xb)+0.2​∑b=15(xb−xb+1)2\sum_{b}(1-x_{b})+0.2\sum_{b=1}^{5}(x_{b}-x_{b+1})^{2}, odd and even blocks form two independent color classes. Enumerating all 64 states and all 64 subsets of proposed edits verifies the merge identity. Enumerating the matching and success outcomes at each state also verifies the expected-drift bound. Across the 4,096 state/subset pairs, the union gives a larger gain than the best color candidate in 1,369 cases and ties in 2,727. Optimistic integration satisfies the merge bound throughout.

Interference on a complete graph.

A concrete instance of Theorem 2 illustrates adverse interactions. For z∈{0,1}mz\in\{0,1\}^{m}, start at z=0z=0 and let each proposal set one coordinate to one under the objective

(29) F⁡(z)≔m−∑b=1mzb+2​∑b<czb​zc.F(z)\coloneqq m-\sum_{b=1}^{m}z_{b}+2\sum_{b<c}z_{b}z_{c}.

Each proposal gains one individually. Applying rr proposals gives

(30) F⁡(0)−F⁡(z)=r−r⁡(r−1)=r⁡(2−r)≤1,F(0)-F(z)=r-r(r-1)=r(2-r)\leq 1,

where r∈{0,…,m}r\in\{0,\ldots,m\}. Thus the best subset gains one out of a total singleton gain of mm, attaining the factor 1/m1/m for the complete graph. For m=2,…,8m=2,\ldots,8, applying all edits gives gain m⁡(2−m)m(2-m), while selecting one color class gives gain one. Optimistic integration therefore selects the color candidate, rejecting the worsening union for m≥3m\geq 3.

The three-agent repair pilot.

Three AI agents independently repaired a parser, discounted-total calculator, and receipt formatter from one common faulty snapshot. Before the original calls we fixed 24 checks: 16 single-function checks and eight adjacent-stage checks. The block-dependency graph is the three-block path, with the two endpoint functions sharing a color. Agents saw the task specification and initial code, not the central checks or other proposals. We replayed the original frozen proposals and made three new calls to the same agents, which retained their earlier task context. The second batch therefore checks repeat behavior with that context available. Both batches gave the same results in Table 20.

The initial singleton gains were 7,4,47,4,4. The best color class gained 11, while the union gained 23, giving an interaction surplus of eight. After the first color-class merge, re-evaluating the stored middle-block proposal raised its gain to 12 and completed the repair without another agent call. Optimistic integration completed repair in one merge, but both verified policies used five objective evaluations. Merge-all used two.

These counts include the initial objective and evaluations of changed singleton candidates; optimistic integration also evaluates the union. Color-candidate loss follows from additivity, and evaluations used only to check that identity are excluded. Thus the pilot illustrates how favorable interactions can save a merge step without reducing verification cost.

For the original proposals, enumerating the eight programs formed by choosing the original or repaired version of each block gives a zero optimum and block-error-bound constant μ=15/23\mu=15/23 on that finite domain. Both batches used the same parent model with different module assignments, and the repeat calls retained the agents’ earlier context. The benchmark in Section 6 reuses this task with six additional hidden checks and starts every call in a fresh context.

Appendix K Extended related work

Graph-theoretic context.

Broader work on graph coloring and related extremal questions includes (Hilton et al., 1973; Demidovich et al., 2023b; Demidovich and Zhukovskii, 2023; Demidovich et al., 2023a; Sagdeev and Raigorodskii, 2019).

Agent systems.

Further work on agent interaction and orchestration includes (Wu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Dang et al., 2025); empirical studies of collaboration include (Cemri et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Park et al., 2026). Ilin and Richtárik (2026) analyze convergence of corrected local search with verified merging.

Distributed optimization and training.

Work on time, allocation, and communication includes (Tyurin and Richtárik, 2023; Maranjyan et al., 2025; Maranjyan and Richtárik, 2026; Fradin et al., 2025). Related work on distributed model training includes (Goyal et al., 2018; Konečný et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024; Li and Richtárik, 2024; Mishchenko et al., 2022; Panferov et al., 2024; Demidovich et al., 2025a; Demidovich et al., 2025b; Sadiev et al., 2022; Sadiev et al., 2025); other optimization and model-adaptation methods include (Khirirat et al., 2025; Sokolov et al., 2025; Ilin and Richtarik, 2025).
